title.narrative: Humanitarian Information Systems, Strengthening evidence-based decision making in South Sudan: HARISS Programme

description.narrative: The humanitarian response is South Sudan is faced with two central issues in terms of information management: 1) ability to regularly monitor humanitarian needs due to accessibility and security issues, inhibiting humanitarian planning and linked to this 2) the ability to effectively prioritise humanitarian assistance, which is becoming ever more urgent in the context of humanitarian needs increasing in severity and in geographic scale. To fill these identified information management gaps, REACH has been collaborating closely and feeding information into the humanitarian architecture in South Sudan to support in tracking of humanitarian needs. Primarily this has been conducted through its AoK remote monitoring (please see Section 4.5) and subsequent information sharing and collaboration with the clusters, the Inter-Cluster Working Group (ICWG) and the Integrated Phase Classification Technical Working Group (IPC TWG). To support improvements in the emergency response prioritization process, in early 2018, REACH played a central role in pushing for shifts in the humanitarian architecture to improve real-time analysis and evidence-based decision making through the set up and co-chairing of the Needs Analysis Working Group (NAWG), tasked with supporting ICWG in emergency response prioritization, and the development of the Integrated Needs Tracking System (INT), tasked by the FSL, WASH, Health and Nutrition clusters to develop an integrated needs monitoring system to support the clusters in prioritizing emergency areas for famine prevention responses.

recipient-country.narrative:
In the context of a widening and deepening humanitarian crisis in South Sudan, with needs escalating both in severity and geographic scale, effective aid prioritization has become an urgent priority. The IPC from October 2018 estimated 59% of South Sudan’s population to face crisis, emergency and catastrophic food insecurity, which makes evidence-based targeting of existing funds a critical necessity to save lives potentially at risk.
At the same time, the dynamic and multi-faceted nature of the South Sudan crisis has created significant challenges for humanitarian information management. Accessibility and security issues within South Sudan have impeded systematic direct data collection efforts – limiting the ability to monitor needs and therefore provide timely information for effective targeting inside the country. As a result, it is becoming increasingly important to adopt adaptive and innovative approaches to filling information gaps in a systematic manner to promote more effective humanitarian response and planning.
